entities.summary:
The University of Salamanca, established in 1218 in Spain, stands as one of the oldest universities in the world and a beacon of intellectual advancement during the Medieval period. Its significance lies not only in its age but also in its role as a pivotal center for the study of law, theology, and the humanities, influencing scholars and institutions across Europe. Key figures such as Francisco de Vitoria and Antonio de Nebrija emerged from its halls, contributing to the development of modern philosophy and linguistics, and its influence extended to the New World, where it shaped colonial education systems.

Throughout the 13th and 14th centuries, the University flourished, attracting students from various regions, including England, France, and Italy. By the late 15th century, it earned a royal charter from Queen Isabella I, further solidifying its prestige. The university played a crucial role in the intellectual debates of the time, particularly in relation to the Spanish Inquisition and the exploration of the Americas, producing groundbreaking works that challenged existing paradigms and promoted humanistic principles.

The legacy of the University of Salamanca is profound, as it laid the foundation for modern university systems across Europe and the Americas. Its emphasis on scholasticism and critical thought influenced subsequent educational reforms, and today it remains a symbol of academic excellence. The university continues to attract scholars and students, reflecting its enduring impact on global education.

As a testament to its historical significance, the University of Salamanca boasts the title of 'the oldest university in the Spanish-speaking world,' having been a critical player in the evolution of higher education and cultural exchange for over eight centuries.

entities.summary: Founded in 1218 by Alfonso IX of León, Salamanca is the oldest university in the Hispanic world and one of the four oldest in Europe. The School of Salamanca (16th century) pioneered international law, developed early economic theory (just price, supply-and-demand), and debated the morality of Spanish colonization. Francisco de Vitoria's work there is the foundation of modern international law.
